description: Looking for team members with varied skills, passionate about astrophysics and coding!
summary: Drift is an interactive, public-facing web application that makes NASA's SPHEREx astronomical data accessible to everyone, encouraging users to explore the sky and identify changes over time. NASA's SPHEREx mission surveys the entire sky in 102 infrared bands, generating an enormous volume of data. Analysing this data and identifying subtle changes presents a significant challenge, creating opportunities for public participation in scientific exploration. Drift addresses this challenge by transforming real SPHEREx observations into an intuitive visual experience. Users can explore different regions of the sky, compare images captured at different times, attempt to spot potential changes in celestial objects and share interesting observations. The platform also incorporates some educational features to help users understand the science behind the data. Furthermore, Drift makes SPHEREx data accessible to everyone and encourages the public to contribute to potential discoveries when in reality the form of data produced by SPHEREx is inaccessible to non-specialists. It also has additional features which further encourage public engagement and comprehension of the data.
details:
Drift is a public-facing web tool that enables users to explore and analyse real data from NASA's SPHEREx mission. The backend accesses the IRSA Archive, using SIA2 to identify relevant observations and IRSA's cutout service to retrieve images for user-selected regions of the sky. The application preserves the World Coordinate System (WCS) metadata, keeping the same relationship between pixels and celestial coordinates.Through the frontend, users can enter Right Ascension (RA) and Declination (Dec), select a few specific celestial objects to view (Barnard’s Star etc.), adjust their field of view and switch between different infrared detector bands.

Benefits:

Drift’s main benefit is that it makes real SPHEREx archive data usable and understandable without hiding where that data came from.

Every visit, FITS cutout, spectrum, and catalogue overlay comes from actual IRSA/ESA archives. There are no synthetic stars, painted differences, or fake fallback frames. That makes it usable for education, outreach, and exploration research.

The viewer turns a stack of archive visits into a playback, A/B blinking, pixel differencing, a real light curve, a change finder, and the new spot-the-difference game. That makes proper motion, variable stars, and brightness changes much easier to notice than in a single image.

Users can pick a named target or enter RA/Dec instead of learning SIA2, TAP, FITS, WCS, and HEALPix first. The app handles discovery, cutouts, wavelength planes, and catalogue overlays behind a UI.

Each frame reports whether it is live IRSA data, cached real data, direct S3 pixels, HiPS context, or a local mirror. The data sources panel probes each service separately. A zero-result field is shown as NO COVERAGE, not filled with fake imagery. 

The six SPHEREx detector bands, measured spectra from WCS-WAVE, HiPS all-sky context, Gaia DR3, and AllWISE overlays let users compare spatial structure, wavelength behavior, and independent catalogues in one place.

The learning lab, constellation lookup, data-verification checks, checksum receipt, and spot-the-difference game turn the archive into something usable in a classroom, planetarium, or public outreach setting. The game in particular teaches that “difference” means measured pixel change, not a decorative puzzle.

The Worker proxy validates product URLs, keeps credentials and upstream calls server-side, caches responsibly, exposes health endpoints, and has tests for the math and mirror integrity. The app is deployable on Render and has a documented local workflow.

The README states what is real and what is limited: the bundled mirror is a sample, not the complete archive; S3 indexing is bounded; HiPS is context only; Gaia is an independent overlay. Those limits are stated rather than papered over.

It benefits the public and students through guided exploration, researchers through quick field inspection and provenance checks, and developers through a working example of a resilient real-data astronomy front end. It is an explorer and outreach tool, not a complete archive ingestion system or a scientific discovery pipeline. Its value comes from making a difficult archive legible, fast to inspect, and honest about its sources.

Intended Impact:

The project aims to make use of the massive volume of data produced by SPHEREx, by increasing opportunities for new celestial discoveries. It also has significant potential to increase the active contribution of the public to astronomical research as well as informing and inspiring users to engage with science. The educational aspects included make astronomy seem more comprehensible and further encourage user engagement.

Tools, language and software:

The live viewer is a lightweight HTML, CSS and JavaScript client, so it opens quickly and doesn't need a heavy framework. ChatGPT was used to assist with frontend desing, coding and debugging. The wider app is React 19 and TypeScript, built with Vite and styled with Tailwind CSS. The API is a Cloudflare Worker using Hono. Node.js and Wrangler handle the build and deploy, and Render hosts the public site. The current backend checks the checked-in S3 spatial index first, then falls back to SIA2/TAP. Cutouts are read from S3 byte ranges first, with the IRSA cutout service as fallback. This is precisely why IRSA web outages no longer break indexed fields.. The browser parses the FITS files and handles the WCS maths. We wrote a dependency-free FITS reader and use astronomy-engine for an independent IAU constellation check. No special hardware is needed. It runs on a normal laptop and browser; the real hardware is the SPHEREx telescope and IRSA's archive. We built it around what a SPHEREx frame actually is: a detector image where position also carries wavelength. Moving across the frame gives you the sky position, wavelength, brightness, flags and pixel scale at that exact point, rather than treating it like a normal photo. The honesty is part of the design. Every frame names its source, and the app keeps live IRSA data, cached data, the verified local mirror and the all-sky context visually separate. If something is context, it says it is context. We turned one dataset into several ways in: a sky map, a visit timeline, blink and difference tools, a change finder, a learning lab and three small games built from real measurements. The all-sky navigation uses the real NASA/JPL-Caltech SPHEREx mosaic, and the games use measured frames. Nothing is simulated just to fill the screen. It still works when IRSA is slow or down. It falls back to a verified local mirror, then to the labelled all-sky context, instead of showing an empty viewer.

What we considered:

- Scientific accuracy came first. We didn't claim a 102-band cube, a

coadd or a proper-motion detection. The 102 channels are 17 channels

across six detector arrays, and the app says that plainly.

- We kept the real WCS and detector orientation. Cutouts aren't

rotated north-up and pixels aren't invented. The native pixel scale is

6.15 arcseconds, and the tool reports what the data actually supports.

- Size and speed mattered. One Level-2 frame is around 72 MB and the

full spectral-image collection is roughly 190 TB, so we request small

cutouts, strip the large PSF block and cache safely instead of

downloading the archive.

- Trust and provenance. The source badge, checksum receipt,

cross-source checks and citations let someone trace a frame back to

IRSA.

- Usability for people who aren't astronomers. We used plain language,

visual cues, keyboard-friendly controls and a responsive layout, then

added the learning lab and games as entry points.

- Failure modes. We planned for IRSA timeouts, empty coverage, partial

data and offline use, with clear states instead of fake fallbacks.

- Scope. We parked coaddition, difference imaging, PSF matching,

proper-motion stacking and a local database because each needs its own

validation. A smaller honest tool was better than a demo that looked

impressive but couldn't be checked.
